about.body: Offhorizon Adventure delivers premium guided motorcycle and self-drive 4x4 expeditions across the Trans-Himalayan region. Every expedition is fully guided, safety-focused, and built for those who want real adventure without compromising on organization or quality.

hero.title: Himalayan expeditions, <accent>done right</accent>.
hero.lead: We plan and lead guided motorcycle and 4x4 expeditions across five countries: the Himalayas of India, Nepal and Bhutan, then Sri Lanka and Mongolia. Ladakh, Spiti Valley, Zanskar, Upper Mustang. Remote country, run with the discipline it demands.

india.title: Motorcycle and 4x4 expeditions across India
india.lead: From the high passes of Ladakh to the cold desert of Spiti, India holds the widest range of adventure riding in the region. We run the northern half of it properly.

intro.title: One country, two entirely different rides.
intro.body: India offers everything from 5,000 metre passes in the north to coastal and cultural routes in the south. They demand different machines, different seasons and different planning.
intro.focus: Our expeditions currently focus on the Indian Himalayas in the north, which is where our workshop, our crew and a decade of terrain knowledge sit. South India is planned, and we will open it when we can run it to the same standard.

permits.q: Do I need travel insurance and permits?
permits.a1: Yes. Both are required, and neither is optional.
permits.a2: Travel insurance is mandatory and must cover:
permits.l2: Motorcycle riding, which many standard policies exclude
permits.a3: The Himalayas are remote. Proper cover is what stands between an incident and a very expensive problem.
permits.a4: Permits are required for several regions, including Ladakh. We arrange all of them, but we need your passport and visa details well in advance to do it.

when.q: When is the riding season in the Indian Himalayas?
when.a1: Broadly June to September, and the edges of that window move every year with the snow.
when.l1: June: passes open, rivers running high from the melt
when.l2: July and August: the most reliable riding, though the monsoon affects the approach through Himachal
when.l3: September: clear skies and the best light, with cold nights
when.a2: Outside that window most high passes are closed. We will tell you if your dates do not work rather than sell you a trip that will not run.

licence.q: What licence do I need to ride in India?
licence.a1: You need a valid motorcycle licence from your home country plus an International Driving Permit, obtained before you travel. An IDP is not issued in India.
licence.a2: Bring the physical documents. A photograph on your phone will not satisfy a checkpoint.

what.a1: The Himalayas are the highest mountain range on earth, running across India, Nepal, Bhutan, China and Pakistan, and forming the barrier between the Indian subcontinent and the Tibetan Plateau.
what.a2: The range holds Mount Everest and more than a hundred peaks above 7,000 metres. The Indus, Ganges and Brahmaputra all rise here and support hundreds of millions of people downstream.
what.a3: For anyone travelling by motorcycle or 4x4, the appeal is the combination of:
what.l1: High mountain passes, several of them among the highest roads in the world
what.l2: Remote off-road trails with days between settlements
what.l3: Landscapes that shift from glacier to cold desert within a single day
what.l4: Living Hindu and Buddhist cultures, not preserved ones
what.a4: We run expeditions in the Indian, Nepalese and Bhutanese Himalayas.

why.q: Why are the Himalayas the best place for a motorcycle expedition?
why.a1: Because few places combine this much altitude, this much remoteness and this much variety in a single trip.
why.a2: Riders get a mix of tarmac, gravel and genuine off-road, on roads that climb past 5,000 metres and through country that sees very few vehicles. Each region reads differently:
why.l1: Ladakh: high passes and extreme, arid landscapes
why.l2: Spiti Valley: remote, raw and technically harder than it looks
why.l3: Upper Mustang in Nepal: trans-Himalayan desert and Tibetan culture
why.l4: Bhutan: quieter roads, dense forest and a slower pace
why.a3: The riding alone would justify the trip. The monasteries, villages and the sheer scale of the place are what people talk about afterwards.

safe.q: Is it safe to ride in the Himalayas?
safe.a1: Yes, when the expedition is planned and staffed properly. The risk here is not the road, it is being unprepared for altitude and distance.
safe.a2: Every expedition travels with an expedition leader, riding guides, a mechanic and a backup vehicle. We also run:
safe.l1: Acclimatisation days before anyone rides high
safe.l2: Daily checks on how each rider is coping with altitude
safe.l3: Oxygen and first aid carried at all times
safe.l4: Routes built from experience rather than from a map
safe.a3: The single most effective safety measure is a schedule with enough slack that nobody feels pressure to ride while unwell.

difficulty.a1: Moderate to challenging, depending on the route.
difficulty.l1: Long riding days between 3,000 and 5,800 metres
difficulty.l2: A mix of smooth tarmac and genuine off-road
difficulty.l3: Weather that can change within an hour
difficulty.l4: Remote sections with no fuel, food or signal
difficulty.a3: They suit riders with basic to intermediate experience and reasonable fitness. With a structured itinerary and a support team, most riders complete the route comfortably.

permits.q: Do I need travel insurance and permits?
permits.a1: Yes. Both are required for every Himalayan expedition.
permits.a2: Travel insurance is mandatory and must cover:
permits.l2: Motorcycle riding, which many standard policies exclude
permits.a3: These are remote regions and evacuation is expensive. Check the exclusions on your policy rather than assuming.
permits.a4: Permits are required for several regions including Ladakh. We arrange all of them, but we need your passport and visa details in advance.
